steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Why FL
  - centralized training prohibitive for many users (clients/agents/workers) sharing large dataset with central server
  - privacy concerns -> sharing may not be feasible
  - so distributed/decentralized training preferred -> federated learning (FL): synergy of large-scale distributed optimization + machine learning
  - much attention in last few years since introduction (cite)
- FL framework (Figure 1)
  - distributed optimization problem, e.g. problem (1), solved with central server + devices exchanging parameters/weights, not private data
  - devices want model trained on data from all devices; local computations, periodically share parameters only
  - minimize finite sum of (usually assumed) differentiable functions depending on data distributions on devices
  - iterative: Step ① clients send local parameters to edge server; Step ② server updates global parameters
  - Steps 2a, 2b specific to our approach: use dataset on edge server
  - Step ③ server broadcasts to all/selected nodes; Step ④ clients update with local (private) data + received global parameters -> next iteration
- One-operator vs three-operator
  - FedAvg (cite), FedProx (cite) = instances of one-operator proximal splitting (cite), i.e. (1) with g\!=\!0; learning mainly on users' side
  - we: three-operator proximal splitting, e.g. our recent TOP-ADMM (three-operator alternating direction method of multipliers) (cite) -> learning on edge server + edge devices
## I-A Motivation
  - future (6G) networks: ML used to design networks and as service provided by them (cite)
  - raw data on users' side and on edge server collocated at base station / radio access networks
  - data generated continuously at physical layer and radio in 5G NR and beyond
  - server + user data -> distributed signal processing: joint communication and sensing, edge learning with Internet of Things
  - FL with learning on server + devices = sum of three functions/operators, see (5)
  - alternatives: block-wise two-operator splitting, or server as virtual user, e.g. two-operator FedADMM (cite)
  - numerically (Figure 5): not necessarily more communication efficient than three-operator perspective
  - to our knowledge, FL with three-operator techniques not addressed; highly novel; datasets from 5G and future 6G
## I-B Contributions
  - FedTOP-ADMM: communication- and computationally efficient FL framework using three-operator ADMM
  - practical edge learning scenario: private datasets on devices + another on edge server/base station; modelled with novel three-operator splitting
  - FedTOP-ADMM by applying/extending TOP-ADMM (cite) to composite problem (5); two variants I and II
    - II: no learning on server side when aggregating; I: learns model before aggregation + in parallel with users -> I slightly better
  - new convergence proof of TOP-ADMM, general convex settings (extends earlier results, cite); optimality conditions of FedTOP-ADMM
  - uses data on edge server at base station -> noticeable communication efficiency gain over state-of-the-art FL on real-world data
  - built on FedADMM framework (cite), inherits its merits; up to 33% more efficient in communication rounds for same target test accuracy vs FedADMM with server data as virtual client

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Centralized training of machine learning models becomes prohibitive when there is a large number of users, especially if the users (also called clients or agents or workers) have to share a large dataset with the central server. Also, some users may not be able to share a dataset with the central server because of privacy concerns. So training algorithms that use distributed and decentralized approaches are preferred. This led to the concept of federated learning (FL), which comes from combining large-scale distributed optimization techniques with machine learning. As a result, FL has received a lot of attention in the last few years since it was introduced.

In the FL framework, shown in Figure 1, a distributed optimization problem such as problem (1) is solved with a central server and other devices, which exchange the parameters/weights of a model instead of sharing private data between them. The devices want to get a learning model that is trained using data from all the other devices. Instead of sending their data to the edge server that computes the model, the devices do some local computations and only share their parameters periodically. More specifically, FL tries to minimize a finite sum of (usually assumed) differentiable functions that depend on the data distributions on the different devices. The usual way to solve this minimization is an iterative procedure. At each global communication iteration the clients send their updated local parameters to a central edge server, which is Step ① in Figure 1. Then the edge server updates the global model parameters, shown as Step ② in Figure 1. The processing Steps 2a and 2b are specific to our proposed approach, and they use the possibility of having a dataset on the edge server to improve the learning model. After that, the server broadcasts the updated parameters or weights to all or to selected nodes, see Step ③ in Figure 1. Finally, the clients update their local parameters using their local (private) dataset and the global model parameters they received from the central server, Step ④ in Figure 1, and the next iteration starts.

Many state-of-the-art FL techniques, like FedAvg and FedProx, can be seen as an instance of one-operator proximal splitting techniques, i.e., described in (1) with function g\!=\!0, which mainly considers learning on the users' side. Unlike these techniques, we propose to go further and use a three-operator proximal splitting technique, such as our recently proposed three-operator alternating direction method of multipliers (TOP-ADMM) method, so that learning can also happen on the edge server together with the usual learning on the edge devices.

## I-A Motivation for Learning Model on the Edge Server
- future (6G) networks: ML used to design networks and as service provided by them (cite)
- raw data on users' side and on edge server collocated at base station / radio access networks; generated continuously at physical layer and radio in 5G NR and beyond
- server + user data -> joint communication and sensing, edge learning with Internet of Things
- FL with learning on server + devices = sum of three functions/operators, see (5)
- alternatives: block-wise two-operator splitting, or server as virtual user (two-operator FedADMM, cite); Figure 5: not necessarily more communication efficient
- to our knowledge not addressed in literature; highly novel; datasets from 5G and future 6G

## I-B Contributions
- FedTOP-ADMM: communication- and computationally efficient FL framework using three-operator ADMM
- edge learning scenario with private datasets on devices + edge server/base station; novel three-operator splitting
- FedTOP-ADMM from TOP-ADMM (cite) for problem (5); variants I and II (I learns before aggregation -> slightly better)
- new convergence proof of TOP-ADMM, general convex settings; optimality conditions of FedTOP-ADMM
- noticeable communication efficiency gain on real-world data
- built on FedADMM (cite); up to 33% fewer communication rounds for same target test accuracy

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Centralized training of machine learning models becomes prohibitive when there is a large number of users, especially if the users (also called clients or agents or workers) have to share a large dataset with the central server. Also, some users may not be able to share a dataset with the central server because of privacy concerns. So training algorithms that use distributed and decentralized approaches are preferred. This led to the concept of federated learning (FL), which comes from combining large-scale distributed optimization techniques with machine learning. As a result, FL has received a lot of attention in the last few years since it was introduced.

In the FL framework, shown in Figure 1, a distributed optimization problem such as problem (1) is solved with a central server and other devices, which exchange the parameters/weights of a model instead of sharing private data between them. The devices want to get a learning model that is trained using data from all the other devices. Instead of sending their data to the edge server that computes the model, the devices do some local computations and only share their parameters periodically. More specifically, FL tries to minimize a finite sum of (usually assumed) differentiable functions that depend on the data distributions on the different devices. The usual way to solve this minimization is an iterative procedure. At each global communication iteration the clients send their updated local parameters to a central edge server, which is Step ① in Figure 1. Then the edge server updates the global model parameters, shown as Step ② in Figure 1. The processing Steps 2a and 2b are specific to our proposed approach, and they use the possibility of having a dataset on the edge server to improve the learning model. After that, the server broadcasts the updated parameters or weights to all or to selected nodes, see Step ③ in Figure 1. Finally, the clients update their local parameters using their local (private) dataset and the global model parameters they received from the central server, Step ④ in Figure 1, and the next iteration starts.

Many state-of-the-art FL techniques, like FedAvg and FedProx, can be seen as an instance of one-operator proximal splitting techniques, i.e., described in (1) with function g\!=\!0, which mainly considers learning on the users' side. Unlike these techniques, we propose to go further and use a three-operator proximal splitting technique, such as our recently proposed three-operator alternating direction method of multipliers (TOP-ADMM) method, so that learning can also happen on the edge server together with the usual learning on the edge devices.

## I-A Motivation for Learning Model on the Edge Server

In future (6G) cellular networks, machine learning services will be used both for designing the networks and as a service that the networks provide. We expect to use the raw data generated not only on the users' side but also on the side of the edge server collocated at the base station and/or radio access networks. More concretely, we see scenarios where the raw data is available at the base station, because data is generated continuously at the physical layer and radio in 5G NR and beyond. So data on the server side together with data on the users' side make many distributed signal processing applications possible, like joint communication and sensing, or edge learning with the Internet of Things (including edge devices). The optimization problem for FL with learning on the edge server and on the edge devices is naturally a sum of three functions or three operators, see (5). Such a three-operator problem for FL could be solved with traditional block-wise two-operator splitting techniques, or by treating the learning model on the edge server as a virtual user, e.g., in the existing two-operator-based FedADMM. However, we show numerically in Figure 5 that this approach is not necessarily more communication efficient than solving the problem from the three-operator proximal splitting perspective.

As far as we know, FL using three-operator techniques, which handles learning on both the server and the users independently, has not been addressed in the literature. This proposal is very novel, and it benefits from the rich datasets available on the edge server and edge devices in current fifth generation (5G) and future 6G cellular networks. These are the key reasons for considering a three-operator problem solved in an FL fashion.

## I-B Contributions

We present a new FL framework that is communication-efficient and computationally efficient, called FedTOP-ADMM, which uses a three-operator ADMM method. Our key contributions are:

- • We show that a practical edge learning scenario is viable, in which private datasets are available on the devices and another private dataset is available on the edge server/base station. We model this scenario with a novel three-operator splitting method that benefits from the private datasets on both the edge server and the edge devices.

- • We propose the FedTOP-ADMM method by applying and extending our recently proposed TOP-ADMM method to a composite optimization problem (5) that is a sum of three functions (or three operators). We propose two variants, FedTOP-ADMM I and FedTOP-ADMM II. FedTOP-ADMM II does not learn on the server side when it aggregates the parameters from the users and the server itself to generate a common model parameter. FedTOP-ADMM I learns a model before the aggregation, in addition to learning in parallel with the users. So FedTOP-ADMM I performs slightly better than FedTOP-ADMM II.

- • We extend our earlier results with a new theoretical convergence proof of TOP-ADMM under general convex settings. Also, by extending the convergence results of TOP-ADMM, we prove the optimality conditions of FedTOP-ADMM.

- • FedTOP-ADMM uses the data that may be available on the edge server collocated at the base station in addition to the data on the users' side. Our numerical experiments with real-world data therefore show a noticeable communication efficiency gain over existing state-of-the-art FL schemes.

- • Our FedTOP-ADMM is built on the existing framework of the communication- and computationally efficient FedADMM, so it inherits all the merits of FedADMM. We also show that FedTOP-ADMM is up to 33% more efficient in terms of communication rounds to reach the same target test accuracy as FedADMM, where the extra dataset on the edge server is modelled as an additional virtual client collocated at the base station.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Centralized training of machine learning models becomes prohibitive for a large number of users, particularly if the users — also known as clients or agents or workers — have to share a large dataset with the central server. Furthermore, sharing a dataset with the central server may not be feasible for some users due to privacy concerns. Training algorithms using distributed and decentralized approaches are therefore preferred. This has led to the concept of federated learning (FL), which results from the synergy between large-scale distributed optimization techniques and machine learning, and FL has received considerable attention in the last few years since its introduction in [1,2].

In the FL framework, illustrated in Figure 1, a distributed optimization problem such as problem (1) is solved by a central server and other devices that exchange the parameters/weights of a considered model rather than sharing private data among themselves. The devices want a learning model trained with data from all the other devices. Instead of sending their data to the edge server that computes such a model, the devices execute some local computations and periodically share only their parameters. Specifically, FL aims to minimize a finite sum of (usually assumed) differentiable functions that depend on the data distributions on the various devices. The common solution is an iterative procedure in which, at each global communication iteration, the clients transmit their updated local parameters to a central edge server (Step ① in Figure 1). The edge server then updates the global model parameters (Step ② in Figure 1); the processing Steps 2a and 2b are specific to our proposed approach and leverage a dataset on the edge server to improve the learning model. The server then broadcasts the updated parameters or weights to all or the selected nodes (Step ③ in Figure 1). Lastly, the clients update their local parameters using their local (private) dataset and the global model parameters received from the central server (Step ④ in Figure 1) and proceed to the next iteration.

Many state-of-the-art FL techniques, such as FedAvg [2] and FedProx [3], can be seen as an instance of one-operator proximal splitting techniques [4], i.e., described in (1) with function g\!=\!0, and mainly consider learning on the users' side. Differently from these techniques, we propose to use a three-operator proximal splitting technique, such as our recently proposed three-operator alternating direction method of multipliers (TOP-ADMM) method [6], to leverage learning on the edge server together with the traditional learning on the edge devices.

## I-A Motivation for Learning Model on the Edge Server

In future (6G) cellular networks, machine learning services will be used both to design the networks and as a service provided by the networks [7]. We expect to leverage raw data generated not only on the users' side but also on the side of the edge server collocated at the base station and/or radio access networks. More concretely, we foresee scenarios in which raw data is available at the base station, since data is generated continuously at the physical layer and radio in 5G NR and beyond. Data on the server side together with data on the users' side thus enable many distributed signal processing applications, such as joint communication and sensing, or edge learning with the Internet of Things (including edge devices). The optimization problem for FL with learning on both the edge server and the edge devices is naturally described by a sum of three functions or three operators — see (5). Such a problem can be solved via traditional block-wise two-operator splitting techniques, or by treating the learning model on the edge server as a virtual user, e.g., in the existing two-operator-based FedADMM [8]. However, we show numerically (see Figure 5) that this approach is not necessarily more communication efficient than tackling the problem from the three-operator proximal splitting perspective.

To the best of our knowledge, FL using three-operator techniques, which tackles learning on both the server and the users independently, has not been addressed in the literature. The proposal is highly novel and benefits from the richly available datasets on the edge server and edge devices in current fifth generation (5G) and future 6G cellular networks. These are the key motivating reasons for tackling a three-operator problem in an FL fashion.

## I-B Contributions

We present a new communication-efficient and computationally efficient FL framework, referred to as FedTOP-ADMM, using a three-operator ADMM method. Specifically, our key contributions are:

- • We demonstrate the viability of a practical edge learning scenario in which private datasets are available on the devices and another private dataset is available on the edge server/base station. We model this scenario using a novel three-operator splitting method that benefits from the private datasets on both edge server and edge devices.

- • We propose the FedTOP-ADMM method by applying and extending our recently proposed TOP-ADMM method [6] to a composite optimization problem (5) comprising a sum of three functions (or three operators). We propose two variants, FedTOP-ADMM I and FedTOP-ADMM II. FedTOP-ADMM II does not learn on the server side when aggregating the parameters from the users and the server itself into a common model parameter, whereas FedTOP-ADMM I learns a model before aggregation in addition to learning in parallel with the users. FedTOP-ADMM I thus performs slightly better than FedTOP-ADMM II.

- • We extend the results of [6] with a new theoretical convergence proof of TOP-ADMM under general convex settings. Additionally, extending the convergence results of TOP-ADMM, we prove the optimality conditions of FedTOP-ADMM.

- • FedTOP-ADMM capitalizes on the data possibly available on the edge server collocated at the base station, in addition to the data on the users' side. Consequently, our numerical experiments on real-world data show a noticeable communication efficiency gain over existing state-of-the-art FL schemes.

- • FedTOP-ADMM is built on the existing framework of the communication- and computationally efficient FedADMM [8] and therefore inherits all its merits. Furthermore, we show that FedTOP-ADMM is up to 33% more efficient in terms of communication rounds to achieve the same target test accuracy as FedADMM, where the extra dataset on the edge server is modelled as an additional virtual client collocated at the base station.
